337.title: Not good to be alone (Genesis 2:18–25)
337.hook: the only thing in creation God calls not good is loneliness
337.howItsDone: Genesis 2:18–24 is one of the Old Testament readings Catholic couples can choose for their wedding Mass, and the Church reads it as the beginning of marriage and of all human community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dust and breath: clay on a workbench and God's breath, face to face. Your line was dust that breathes. When did you feel both halves? A new week starts. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

Count the verdicts so far. Light: good. Dry land and sea: good. Plants: good. Sun, moon and stars: good. Fish and birds, cattle and creeping things: good. Everything together: very good. Genesis keeps saying it like a bell. And then, in the garden, with the first human freshly made and a whole world to tend, the bell rings wrong. God looks at the man and says something is not good. Not sin. Nothing has gone wrong yet. No serpent, no fruit. Just one person, by himself, in paradise.
screen: `GOOD, GOOD, GOOD, VERY GOOD.` → `THE BELL RINGS WRONG.` → `ONE PERSON, BY HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the line in the Douay-Rheims: "It is not good for man to be alone: let us make him a help like unto himself." First, the problem. The first thing in the Bible called not good isn't evil. It's being alone. The man has God, a garden and work, and still something is missing. Second, the word help. In Hebrew it's ezer kenegdo, a helper corresponding to him, one who stands facing him. Ezer is not a servant's word. The Hebrew Bible uses it most often for God, who is Israel's help. So the help God promises isn't an assistant. It's a partner, an equal, someone who can look back. Third, the search. God brings the animals to the man, and he names every one. Cattle, birds, beasts of the field. But none of them is the help like himself. Then God casts the man into a deep sleep, takes one of his ribs, closes up the flesh, and builds a woman. When he wakes and sees her, the first human words in the Bible spill out, and they're close to a song: this now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. Fourth, how the Church reads it. The Catechism says man and woman are made for each other, a communion of persons, and that this is where marriage begins. But the Church also reads the line more widely: no human being is made to be alone. Friendship, family, parish, neighbors: all of them answer the same not good. And the garden scene ends quietly. They were both naked, and were not ashamed.
screen: `THE FIRST NOT GOOD: ALONE.` · `EZER: A HELP, LIKE GOD IS.` · `NO ANIMAL IS LIKE HIMSELF.` · `BONE OF MY BONES.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT GOOD FOR MAN TO BE ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reach out to someone alone. Settle, and breathe. Let a face come to mind: someone living by themselves, a widower down the street, a friend who moved to a new city, a coworker who eats lunch at the desk, an older relative whose phone doesn't ring much. Stay with that one person. Picture where they are right now, what the room sounds like. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. After the bell, send one message or make one call. Nothing big. Just proof that someone thought of them. The bell holds the time.
Not good to be alone. The first not good in the Bible: one person, by himself. God's answer is a help like himself, an equal who stands facing him.
screen: `NOT GOOD TO BE ALONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not good to be alone. Today, notice who's on the edge of the room, the group chat or the table, and pull them one step in. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

338.title: The serpent (Genesis 3:1–7)
338.hook: did God really say, and the fruit that looked good
338.howItsDone: Catholics pray "lead us not into temptation" in every Our Father, and the Church reads Genesis 3 on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, as Lent begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not good to be alone: the first not good, and an equal who stands facing him. Who did you pull one step in? Today, the garden gets a visitor. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

Picture the most famous painting of this scene you can think of. There's probably a tree, a woman reaching up, and a shiny red apple. Maybe a snake curled around a branch, with a face. Now open Genesis and look for the apple. It isn't there. The text just says fruit. The apple seems to have grown later, in art, perhaps helped along by a Latin pun: malum means evil, and malum also means apple. The real story is quieter and stranger than the paintings. It doesn't start with a bite. It starts with a question.
screen: `A TREE, A WOMAN, A RED APPLE.` → `THE TEXT SAYS ONLY FRUIT.` → `IT STARTS WITH A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The serpent, Genesis says, was more subtle than any of the beasts. And its first words are a question. In the Douay-Rheims: "Why hath God commanded you, that you should not eat of every tree of paradise?" Other translations put it more sharply: did God really say? Notice the trick. God had said they could eat of every tree but one. The serpent turns the one limit into the whole story. The woman corrects it, but now the doubt is in the air. Then the serpent goes further: you won't die; God knows that you'll be like gods. That's the shape of temptation the Church sees here. First, the question that shrinks the gift and enlarges the rule. Second, the suspicion: maybe God is holding out on you. Third, the look. The woman sees that the tree is good to eat, fair to the eyes, and desirable for wisdom. Everything about it looks good. Temptation rarely shows up looking evil. Fourth, the result. She eats, gives some to her husband, who is with her, and he eats. Their eyes are opened, but what they see is only that they're naked. They sew fig leaves. The Catechism reads this as the first sin: letting trust in God die in the heart, and wanting to be like God without God. It uses figurative language, the Catechism says, but it tells of a real event at the start of human history. And Genesis never names the serpent. Later scripture, the Book of Wisdom and Revelation, identifies it with the devil.
screen: `A QUESTION THAT SHRINKS THE GIFT.` · `MAYBE GOD IS HOLDING OUT.` · `IT LOOKS GOOD TO THE EYES.` · `TRUST DIES BEFORE THE BITE.` · then, large: `DID GOD REALLY SAY?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one small temptation's voice. Settle, and breathe. Think of something small you keep doing that you'd rather not: the third episode, the snapped reply, the extra purchase, the scroll at midnight. Now listen for the sentence that comes right before it. It's usually reasonable. You deserve this. It doesn't really matter. Nobody will know. Just hear it, without arguing back. Notice how gentle it sounds. If you pray, you can ask for help to recognize it next time. The bell holds the time.
Temptation. Being drawn toward a wrong that looks good. In the garden it starts with a question that makes the gift look small and the limit look huge.
Your line: did god really say. Today, when a little voice says the rule doesn't count this time, name the trick out loud, even silently, and pause for three breaths. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

339.title: Where art thou (Genesis 3:8–13)
339.hook: God walks in the garden in the cool of the day and calls for the hiding couple
339.howItsDone: In the sacrament of reconciliation, Catholics name their own sins aloud to a priest, rather than explaining others' faults, and receive absolution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, temptation: a question that makes the gift look small. Your line was did god really say. Did you catch the trick anywhere? Today, what happens right after the bite. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

A kid breaks a vase. Their parent hears the crash from the kitchen and walks into the living room, and the room is empty. Except for two small feet sticking out from behind the curtain. The parent knows exactly where the child is. Everyone in the room knows. And still the parent says, out loud, gently or not: where are you? That's the scene in Genesis today. The fruit is eaten. The fig leaves are sewn. And the evening breeze comes through the garden, and with it, the sound of someone walking.
screen: `A CRASH, AN EMPTY ROOM.` → `TWO FEET BEHIND THE CURTAIN.` → `SOMEONE WALKING IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: First, the walk. Genesis says the man and the woman heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden, in the afternoon air, the cool of the day. It's an astonishingly close picture of God: not thunder, but footsteps at evening, as if this were a habit. And they hide among the trees. Second, the question. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord God called Adam, and said to him: Where art thou?" In Hebrew it's one word, ayekkah. God made the man from dust. God isn't asking for directions. Jewish and Christian teachers have noticed this for centuries: the question isn't for God's information. It's for Adam. It gives him a chance to come out on his own. Third, the answer, and it's painfully honest: "I heard thy voice in paradise; and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." Afraid, naked, hid. Three words that describe a lot of human life. Fourth, the blame. God asks who told him he was naked, and whether he ate. And the man points: the woman you gave me, she gave me the fruit. Notice he blames her and, quietly, God too. The woman points at the serpent. Nobody says I did it. The Catechism says the harmony of the garden is broken here: between the man and woman, with creation, and with God. And yet the first word God speaks to a sinner in the Bible is not a sentence. It's a question that goes looking for him. Catholics hear the same call in confession: come out from behind the trees and say it.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS IN THE EVENING AIR.` · `AYEKKAH: ONE WORD, A QUESTION.` · `AFRAID, NAKED, HID.` · `NOBODY SAYS I DID IT.` · then, large: `WHERE ART THOU?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: come out from one hiding place. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself the old question, slowly: where are you? Not your location. Where are you hiding? Maybe behind being busy. Behind a joke. Behind a story where it was mostly someone else's fault. Pick one. Just one tree you've been standing behind. Picture taking one step out from it, into the open air. Nobody's shouting. It's evening, and someone is calling your name. If you pray, you can answer with Adam's honest words, I was afraid. The bell holds the time.
Where art thou. Ayekkah in Hebrew: the first question God asks in the Bible, spoken to a man hiding in the trees. Not for information. An invitation.
Your line: where art thou. Today, when you catch yourself about to blame someone, stop one sentence earlier and say what you did instead. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

340.title: The first good news (Genesis 3:15)
340.hook: even in the curse, a promise that the woman's seed will crush the serpent; Catholics see Christ and Mary here
340.howItsDone: Genesis 3:9–15, 20 is read at Mass on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, December 8, and many Catholic images of Mary show the serpent under her feet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, where art thou: footsteps in the evening and a question that went looking for someone hiding. Did you stop one sentence before blaming? Day three hundred forty.

Walk into almost any old Catholic church and look for a statue of Mary. Very often she's standing on a globe, hands open or folded, and under her bare feet, crushed flat, there's a snake. Sometimes it has an apple in its mouth. People walk past it every Sunday without a second look. But that snake under her heel is a Bible verse turned into stone. It comes from the darkest moment in Genesis so far: the fruit eaten, the blame passed around, God about to speak the consequences. And right there, before any of the hard news, comes a promise.
screen: `MARY ON A GLOBE.` → `A SNAKE UNDER HER HEEL.` → `A VERSE TURNED INTO STONE.`

segments.voice: God speaks first to the serpent, and says this, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel." First, the order. Before God says a word to the man or the woman about pain and sweat and dust, God promises that evil won't win. The promise comes before the punishment. Second, the name. Christians since at least the second century, Irenaeus among them, read this verse as the first announcement of Christ, and so it came to be called the protoevangelium, the first gospel, the first good news. The woman's seed is a descendant who will crush the serpent's head, while the serpent only strikes the heel. A wound, but not a fatal one. Third, the word she. Here's something careful readers should know. The Hebrew says he, or it, the offspring. The Greek Old Testament says he. Saint Jerome's Latin Vulgate has ipsa, she, and the Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin, follows it. Most modern translations, Catholic ones included, follow the Hebrew. Fourth, how the Church holds both. The Catechism reads the verse as pointing to Christ, the new Adam, and to Mary, the new Eve, who shares in his victory. So the Church doesn't need to choose between he and she: the Son crushes the serpent, and his mother stands with him. That's the statue. Not a woman fighting alone, but the first promise in the Bible, carved in stone and placed where you'd pass it.
screen: `THE PROMISE BEFORE THE PUNISHMENT.` · `PROTOEVANGELIUM: FIRST GOOD NEWS.` · `HE IN HEBREW, SHE IN THE LATIN.` · `THE NEW ADAM AND THE NEW EVE.` · then, large: `SHE SHALL CRUSH THY HEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find hope inside a hard moment. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something hard that's happening now, yours or someone else's. Don't pretend it's fine. Let it be as heavy as it is. Then look inside it, the way Genesis tucks a promise into the curse. Is there one small thing that's still good, still possible, still on its way? A friend who showed up. A door not fully closed. A morning that will come anyway. Hold that one thing next to the hard thing. If you pray, you can hand both to God. The bell holds the time.
Protoevangelium. Proto, first; evangelium, gospel. The name Christians give Genesis three fifteen: the first good news, spoken in the middle of the fall.
Your line: the promise came first. Today, when you have to deliver bad news, or hear it, look for the promise to say before it. Day three hundred forty.

341.title: Am I my brother's keeper (Genesis 4:1–16)
341.hook: Cain kills Abel and God still puts a mark of protection on him
341.howItsDone: In the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer, the priest asks God to accept the offering as he accepted the gifts of Abel the just, the sacrifice of Abraham and the offering of Melchizedek.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the protoevangelium: a promise spoken before the punishment. Your line was the promise came first. Did you find one to say before hard news? Now, outside the garden, the first family. Day three hundred forty-one.

There's a line people quote all the time without knowing where it comes from. A politician uses it in a speech. A teacher writes it on a board. Someone mutters it when asked to help a neighbor: what am I, my brother's keeper? It sounds like a shrug. It's actually a lie, told to God's face, by the first person in the Bible to kill another. Two brothers, the first children born outside Eden. One works the soil, one keeps sheep. They both bring an offering. And one of them doesn't come home.
screen: `A LINE EVERYONE QUOTES.` → `IT'S A LIE, TOLD TO GOD.` → `TWO BROTHERS, ONE OFFERING EACH.`

segments.voice: First, the offerings. Cain brings fruit of the ground; Abel brings the firstlings of his flock. God has respect to Abel's offering and not to Cain's. Why? Genesis doesn't say. The text is silent, and readers have guessed for centuries. The Letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered by faith. Second, the warning. Cain's face falls, and God speaks to him before anything happens: sin lies at the door, but you can master it. God sees the anger and talks to him about it. Cain doesn't answer. He takes his brother into the field and kills him. Third, the question. Like in the garden, God asks something God already knows. In the Douay-Rheims: "Where is thy brother Abel? And he answered, I know not: am I my brother's keeper?" Adam hid. Cain lies, and then shrugs. And God says: "The voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth." The ground that took Adam's sweat now drinks a brother's blood. The Catechism quotes this scene when it teaches about the sacredness of every human life. Fourth, the surprise. Cain is sent out as a wanderer, and he's afraid someone will kill him. And God puts a mark on him, not a brand of shame, but a sign of protection: nobody is to take his life. Even for a murderer, God keeps the door open. Catholics remember Abel at the altar: the Roman Canon names the offering of Abel the just. And the answer to Cain's question, the whole Bible says, is yes.
screen: `WHY ABEL'S? THE TEXT IS SILENT.` · `SIN LIES AT THE DOOR.` · `THY BROTHER'S BLOOD CRIETH.` · `A MARK OF PROTECTION.` · then, large: `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check on a brother or sister. That might be a sibling by blood, or someone who's been one to you. Settle, and breathe. Let their face come. Where are they this week? What's hard for them right now, as far as you know? If there's distance between you, notice it without blaming anyone. Just hold them. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. After the bell, send something small: how are you, really? The bell holds the time.
Am I my brother's keeper. Cain's answer to God's question after he killed Abel: a lie, and a shrug. The rest of the Bible keeps answering it.
screen: `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: yes, you are. Today, when you're tempted to say that's not my problem about someone near you, do one small thing for them instead. Day three hundred forty-one.

342.title: Noah builds (Genesis 6–7)
342.hook: a righteous man builds a boat under a clear sky
342.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, the priest's blessing of the baptismal water recalls the flood as a sign of baptism, and Catholics have long pictured the Church as an ark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, am I my brother's keeper: a lie, a shrug, and a mark of protection. Your line was yes, you are. Who did you do one small thing for? Day three hundred forty-two.

A man in a quiet neighborhood starts building a boat in his backyard. Not a canoe. A ship, longer than a football field, three decks high, nowhere near any water. Day after day, the sound of saws. Months. Years. Neighbors would have opinions. The famous retellings of Noah are full of them: mocking crowds, jokes, a lonely builder. Genesis never mentions a single neighbor's reaction. Not one word. What it gives us instead is a man, an instruction, and a long, plain list of measurements.
screen: `A SHIP IN THE BACKYARD.` → `NO WATER IN SIGHT.` → `GENESIS: NOT ONE NEIGHBOR'S WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the world. By chapter six, the story says the earth is corrupt and filled with violence, and God is grieved at heart. Cain's one murder has become a whole culture. Second, the man. In the Douay-Rheims: "Noe was a just and perfect man in his generations, he walked with God." Noe is the old Latin spelling of Noah. He walked with God, the same phrase Genesis used for Enoch. Third, the instruction. God tells him to make an ark of timber planks, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high, roughly four hundred fifty feet, with rooms and a window and a door in the side. The Hebrew word for ark, tevah, appears in only one other story in the Bible: the little basket the baby Moses floats in on the Nile. A giant ship and a reed basket, the same word. Both carry someone through the water to a new beginning. Fourth, what Noah does, and this is the whole point of the chapter: "And Noe did all things which God commanded him." Genesis says it more than once. No speech, no argument. He builds. Then the rain comes, forty days and forty nights, and the ark lifts off the ground. From early on, Christians read the ark as more than a boat. The First Letter of Peter compares the flood waters to baptism, and Church Fathers saw the ark as the Church, carrying people safely through. The flood is still named in the Easter Vigil's blessing of the baptismal water. A man building under a clear sky, because he trusted the one who told him to.
screen: `THE EARTH FILLED WITH VIOLENCE.` · `HE WALKED WITH GOD.` · `TEVAH: A SHIP AND A BASKET.` · `NOE DID ALL THINGS.` · then, large: `BUILD UNDER A CLEAR SKY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one faithful thing nobody understands. Settle, and breathe. Think of a good thing you've been putting off because it looks odd, or pointless, or too slow to matter: writing to someone who never writes back, saving for something far away, going to Mass alone, practicing an instrument nobody hears. Let the reasons not to come up, and let them pass. Picture yourself doing the first plank of it. If you pray, you can ask for Noah's kind of steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Noah builds. A just man who walked with God, building an ark with no water in sight, and doing all things God commanded him.
Your line: build anyway. Today, lay one plank of something good that won't pay off for a long time: ten minutes, one page, one coin set aside. Day three hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 342 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BOW IN THE CLOUDS.`

343.title: The bow in the clouds (Genesis 8–9)
343.hook: after the flood, God's promise with every living thing
343.howItsDone: The Church reads God's covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:8–15) on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, and the Catechism describes it as God's covenant with all the nations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Noah builds: a ship under a clear sky, and a man who did all things God commanded. Your line was build anyway. What plank did you lay? Day three hundred forty-three, the end of the week.

A hundred and fifty days, the water rules the earth. Then it begins to fall. The ark grounds on the mountains of Ararat. Noah opens the window and sends out a raven, which flies back and forth. Then a dove, which finds nowhere to land and comes back to his hand. He waits seven days and sends her again, and at evening she returns with an olive leaf in her beak. Seven days more, and she doesn't come back at all. That olive branch in a dove's beak is still on flags and posters and peace signs everywhere. But the story isn't finished when the ground dries.

segments.voice: First, the word. Covenant, in Hebrew berit, is a binding promise between two parties, more than a contract, closer to a family bond. It appears here for the first time in Genesis in full. Second, who's in it. Not just Noah. God makes it with Noah, his sons, their children after them, and, the text keeps saying, every living creature: birds, cattle, beasts of the earth, everything that came out of the ark. The animals are named as partners in a promise. Third, what's promised: never again will a flood destroy the earth. And the sign. In the Douay-Rheims: "I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant between me, and between the earth." The Hebrew word for bow, qeshet, is the ordinary word for a warrior's bow. Many readers see a picture here: God hanging up the weapon, pointed away from the earth. That's an image readers have drawn, not something the text spells out. But the text is clear about who the sign is for: when the bow appears, God says, I will remember. The reminder is for God. Fourth, why the Church cares. The Catechism calls this covenant with Noah the start of God's long plan of salvation, one that stays in force for all the nations, everyone, until the gospel goes out to the whole world. And it closes a week that began with a lonely man in a garden, a serpent's question, a call into the trees, the first good news, a brother's blood, an ark, and now color across the sky.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for color in the sky. If you can see a window, look out of it now. If not, picture the last sky you noticed. Settle, and breathe. Find whatever color is there: blue, gray, the orange edge of a cloud, the dull white of an overcast day. Let your eyes rest on it. Then think of every creature under that same sky right now: birds, a neighbor's dog, a stray cat, a fish you'll never see, a stranger across the world. All of them, in the story, inside one promise. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Covenant. Berit in Hebrew: a binding promise. After the flood, God makes one with Noah and every living creature, and sets a bow in the clouds as its sign.
